July 12, 2023 Thoreau Statue Henry David Thoreau, American naturalist, essayist, poet, and philosopher, is considered an early environmentalist as his writings on natural history and philosophy foresaw the methods and findings of ecology and environmental history. Thoreau’s classic book Walden or Life in the Woods, written in 1854, compresses his two years, two months, and two days living self-sufficiently alone at Walden Pond into one calendar year with the four seasons symbolizing human development. This statue portrays Henry David Thoreau in front of his reconstructed cabin at Walden Pond, near Concord, Massachusetts. July 19, 2023 Burmese Temple The Shwenandaw Kyaung Temple, built in traditional Burmese architectural style, is the only remaining structure from the original Royal Palace in Amarapura. The temple was later moved to nearby Mandalay where is remains today. After King Mindo died in the building in 1878, it was converted into a monastery dedicated to his memory. The monastery is known for its teak carvings of Buddhist myths adorning the walls and roof. July 26, 2023 Mangrove Forest Mangrove forest ecosystems are crucial to the environment. Mangrove forests remove five times more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere than terrestrial forests. The largest mangrove forest in the world is the Sundarbans National Park in India, which is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a World Network of Biosphere Reserve. August 02, 2023 Peacock Mosaic Pictured is a mosaic of a peacock in the House of Dionysos (so named because many of the mosaics there relate to the worship of the god Dionysos) at the Paphos Archeological Park located in southwest Cyprus. At this ancient Greek and Roman coastal city the most significant remains discovered so far are four large Roman villas: the House of Dionysos, the House of Aion, the House of Theseus, and the House of Orpheus all of which have well-preserved mosaic floors. Paphos became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1980. August 31, 2023 Issyk-Kul (Warm Lake) VIEW 30-DAY ARCHIVE What's New The classic science fiction adventure novel, Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, is one of Jules Verne's most famous and popular works. The title refers to the distance, not depth, traveled under various seas. A league is a unit of measure no longer used in today's World, but how far is 20,000 leagues converted to kilometers or nautical miles? Find the answer by consulting Appendix G: Weights and Measures. (Hint: the distance is more than twice the circumference of the Earth.)

September 28, 2023 Tangier, Morocco VIEW 30-DAY ARCHIVE What's New The World Factbook is delighted to announce the addition of a new "Wonders of the World" field under World > Geography. This entry presents information on three groups of Wonders: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, The New Seven Wonders of the World, and The World Factbook's Seven Natural Ultra-Wonders of the World. The latter is the only entry in The World Factbook that has been independently compiled by the Factbook's staff and is not derived from some other source. The listing is one of 'Ultra-Wonders' because it consists of natural phenomena/spectacles that are the largest in their respective categories and thus cannot be exceeded. Check out the compilation, some of the Wonders may surprise you.

October 05, 2023 Vanuatu Flag VIEW 30-DAY ARCHIVE What's New On September 25, 2023, the United States recognized two Pacific Ocean self-governing entities in free association with New Zealand - the Cook Islands and Niue - as sovereign and independent states, bringing the total number of countries in The World Factbook to 197. The free association status of the Cook Islands and Niue allows for a great deal of internal autonomy, but transfers responsibility for defense and foreign affairs to New Zealand. This status is similar to the free association relationship that the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau (three other Pacific island entities) enjoy with the United States and that are also recognized as independent countries.

November 02, 2023 Hermit Crabs VIEW 30-DAY ARCHIVE What's New The World Factbook has added a new appendix on language codes that includes two- and three-character codes. Language codes are critical in place names data where a single place may have multiple names or spellings from different languages. The new appendix designation is D-3: Language Data Codes and it joins two other data code entries, D-1: Country Data Codes (formerly Appendix D) and D-2: Hydrographic Data Codes (formerly Appendix E). The Factbook now includes 12 useful appendices.

November 30, 2023 Barbados VIEW 30-DAY ARCHIVE What's New The World Factbook contains descriptions of the population distribution for the World, countries, and territories. Globally, six of the world's seven continents are widely and permanently inhabited. Asia is easily the most-populous continent with about 60% of the world's population (China and India together comprise over 35%), while Africa comes in second with over 15% of the earth's populace. Europe accounts for about 10%, North America 8%, South America almost 6%, and Oceania less than 1%. The harsh conditions on Antarctica prevent any permanent habitation.

February 29, 2024 Leap Day VIEW 30-DAY ARCHIVE What's New This Caribbean Island nation and self-governing territory of the UK introduced its current flag on May 30, 1990. It features the British flag in the upper hoist-side quadrant, recognizing the country’s relationship with the UK, and the national coat of arms in the center depicting three orange dolphins in an interlocking circular design jumping out of the sea, represented by a turquoise-blue field below them. The three dolphins, adopted from this island nation’s earlier Three Dolphin Flag, reflect the national motto: Unity, Strength, and Endurance. The dolphin is also a national symbol, and their circular arrangement on the flag represents continuity. Can you name this country? (hint: please refer to the Flags of the World page and the National Symbols page)

March 07, 2024 Phuoc Duyen Tower VIEW 30-DAY ARCHIVE What's New The UN has declared 2024 the International Year of Camelids to highlight how these animals are essential to the livelihoods and survival of millions of households (particularly indigenous families) in mountainous, arid, and semi-arid environments in more than 90 countries. The Camelidae family includes the vicuna, alpaca (domesticated form of vicuna), guanaco, and llama (domesticated form of guanaco) native to South America and the dromedary camel, Bactrian camel, and wild camel found in Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Known for their cultural and social significance, the alpaca (pictured) and the llama have been used by native peoples in Peru and other parts of the Andes Mountains for thousands of years as work animals and sources of meat, fiber, milk, and fertilizer. Camelid wool is a mainstay of Peru's textile and clothing industries. To learn more about the industries of Peru and other countries, please visit The World Factbook's industries page.

March 21, 2024 Lake Toba VIEW 30-DAY ARCHIVE What's New Desert covers about 70% of this landlocked, sparsely populated African country. Its Okavango Delta is one of the few inland delta systems that does not flow into a sea or ocean. Instead, its waters drain into the sands of the Kalahari Basin. The delta is one of the most biodiverse areas in Africa and sustains robust populations of some of the world’s most endangered large mammals, including the cheetah, white and black rhinoceros, wild dog, and lion. The Okavango Delta was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014. (hint: please refer to the Geography - note page and the National heritage page)
